Only one number measures whether the customer came back. Key takeaways Standard resolution metrics grade the case, not the relationship. They can improve in the same quarter that repeat purchase falls. The repeat-purchase gap is the difference between how often shoppers who had an order problem buy again and how often shoppers who had no problem buy again. About 71% of consumers say they are less likely to shop with a retailer again after a poor returns experience, up from 67% a year earlier. The cost of a poor resolution lands a purchase cycle later, not in this month's support numbers. The gap is worth cutting by resolution outcome, issue type, and trust tier. That is where it stops being a scorecard and starts being an operating lever. Pull up your resolution dashboard and most of it reads well. Average time-to-resolution is down. CSAT on closed cases sits above four. Deflection is climbing, so the team is handling more volume without more headcount. Every number on the board says the resolution experience is working. Now ask a question the board can't answer: Of the shoppers who had a problem with an order last quarter, a delay, a missing box, a damaged item, a return, how many of them bought from you again? And how does that rate compare with shoppers who had no problem at all? Most enterprise retailers can't produce that comparison on demand, which is a problem, because it is the only number that tells you whether resolution is doing its actual job. Your post-purchase resolution metrics grade the case, not the customer Time-to-resolution, first-contact resolution, CSAT, and deflection rate share a design assumption: that a case closed cleanly is a case that worked. Each one measures the mechanics of shutting a ticket. None of them measures what the shopper does next. That gap between the two is significant. A fast, generous cash refund closes the case in under an hour, scores well on CSAT, requires no agent time, and hands the shopper their money back along with a good reason to shop somewhere less risky next time. On your dashboard, that is a win. In your revenue, it is churn with good manners. The size of the effect is well documented, and it is growing. About 71% of consumers now say they are less likely to shop with a retailer again after a poor returns experience, up from 67% the year before. Four out of five say they tell friends and family about it. And the pattern holds earlier in the journey too: Narvar platform data shows shoppers whose order arrived inside the promised delivery window go on to repurchase at 42.9%, against 12.6% for shoppers who watched that window pass. A three-fold difference in future revenue, driven by one experience, and none of it visible in a support metric. Shoppers won't remember the claim process. They'll remember how resolution felt. Your ticket metrics don’t capture that sentiment. The repeat-purchase gap, defined Your own no-issue cohort is the benchmark. There is no useful industry average here, because the number moves with category, price point, and purchase frequency. What matters is the distance between your two cohorts and which direction it travels quarter over quarter. A narrow, narrowing gap means recovery is working. A wide one is revenue leaving through a door nobody is watching. Three details make the measurement honest. First, use a fixed window on both sides: 90 days after order date works for most categories and 180 for considered purchases. Second, split the issue population into two cohorts rather than one: shoppers whose issue reached a resolution, and shoppers who reported an issue and abandoned it. That second group is usually small, rarely tracked, and repurchases at a rate that will get an executive's attention. Third, run it on order-level data, not ticket-level, because the shopper who solved their problem in self-service never opened a ticket and belongs in the analysis just as much as the one who called. Then cut the gap three ways, which is where it turns into something you can act on: By resolution outcome , so you can see whether an exchange, a store credit, a replacement, or a cash refund produces different repurchase behavior on the same issue type. By issue type , so a damaged-item problem isn't averaged together with a fit-driven return. And by trust tier , so you find out whether your highest-value shoppers are getting your fastest resolutions or your most cautious ones. Want a read on your resolution experience? The Resolution Confidence Assessment scores you across four signals in about five minutes, no demo required. Take the quiz . Four moves that close the gap 1. Take the handoffs out. Shoppers don't sort problems the way your org chart does. 32% blame a late delivery on both the carrier and the retailer, and another 21% don't care who is at fault as long as it gets fixed ( Narvar, 2025 State of Post-Purchase Report ). When someone is pushed from support to a carrier page to a separate returns portal, they read those seams as your brand failing them, and they price that into the next order. Connecting claims, returns, and delivery exceptions onto one path is the single change that moves the gap most, because it removes the friction the shopper actually remembers. 2. Match the outcome to the issue. A delayed package needs a proactive update and a revised delivery estimate, nothing more. A damaged item needs a replacement or a claim, and a missed holiday gift needs both of those faster than the same issue in February. When every issue type runs through one general process, most shoppers get an outcome that is close enough to be technically correct and far enough off to be remembered as a hassle. 3. Tell trusted shoppers from risky ones in real time. Fraud is a real constraint on how generous you can afford to be. 15.14% of 2024 returns were deemed fraudulent, and fraudulent returns and claims together cost retailers $103 billion. But abuse concentrates in a small share of shoppers, and designing the whole flow around the worst case taxes everyone else. Reserve verification, held refunds, and inspection for genuine...

blogs.content: Singles’ Day 2025 marketing playbook Generated by Klaviyo AI This article explains what makes Singles’ Day different from BFCM and why it’s a growing opportunity for ecommerce brands worldwide. It outlines creative campaign ideas, from self-gifting bundles and gamification to VIP experiences and referral promos, and shows how Klaviyo features support segmentation, personalization, and automation for Singles’ Day. Singles’ Day fundamentals: Learn how Singles’ Day evolved into a self-gifting, experience-driven shopping event distinct from Black Friday Cyber Monday and why it’s gaining traction beyond China. Creative campaign ideas: Explore eight Singles’ Day tactics, including personalized self-gifting offers, gamified experiences, 11-themed promotions, Singles’ Week warm-ups, VIP treatments, limited editions, referrals, and self-love storytelling. Segmentation and personalization: See how to use zero- and first-party data, quizzes, and behavioral signals to build intent-based segments for self-gifters and gift buyers and tailor Singles’ Day messaging accordingly. Klaviyo-powered execution: Understand how Klaviyo’s segmentation, dynamic content, flows, predictive analytics, and integrations with quizzes, UGC, and referral tools can operationalize Singles’ Day strategies across channels. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary According to data from Syntun shared via EMARKETER , Singles’ Day 2025 generated $236.60 billion USD (RMB 1.695 trillion) in China, a 17.5% YoY increase from 2024. To put that number into perspective, Black Friday in the US drove $11.8 billion in sales in 2025, according to Adobe Analytics . Singles’ Day is massive in markets outside the US, especially in Australia, New Zealand, Southeast Asia, and Europe. But global brands are starting to realize the potential for Singles’ Day, with 32% of US consumers aware of the holiday, according to Statista . Singles’ Day, also known as Double 11, first kicked off in China as a kind of anti-Valentine’s Day. It started back in the 1990s when university students decided to celebrate being single on November 11. (Get it? 11/11, or 4 “ones” for 4 single people.) What began as a tongue-in-cheek celebration quickly turned into the biggest shopping event in the world when Alibaba jumped on board in the 2000s and made it a mega ecommerce moment. The one-day event is a discount-driven event like Black Friday Cyber Monday (BFCM)—it’s even in the same month. But it’s a different beast entirely. While BFCM is mostly about buying gifts for others or prepping for Christmas , Singles’ Day is rooted in self-gifting. That shift in mindset means there are some unique opportunities to promote products as indulgent, fun, or emotionally supportive. As Singles’ Day gains traction outside of China, we’re seeing 3 global trends: Economic uncertainty is shaping shopping habits. With consumer optimism at a two-year low and rising prices topping shoppers' concerns, according to McKinsey , people are spending more selectively. So, offers that emphasize value, flexibility (like bundles or payment plans), and emotional benefit may land better. Younger audiences get it. Brands in markets outside of China see Singles’ Day as an opportunity to connect with younger, mobile-first shoppers who are used to shopping events that feel like experiences. Brands are starting early. Campaigns are launching weeks in advance to warm up audiences, gather wishlists, and reward VIPs. Because this holiday is all about self-love and indulgence, it’s a great opportunity to break out of your usual promo playbook and create experiences that feel fun, empowering, and totally personal. Here are 8 creative angles you can explore. 1. Personalize Singles’ Day offers for single shoppers Rather than blasting out a generic discount, make your Singles’ Day campaign feel a little more thoughtful with personalized gifts and offers. Start by identifying customers who are most likely to vibe with the “treat yourself” mindset, like solo travelers, skincare lovers, or anyone who’s shown an interest in a product that screams self-care. Here are some personalized Singles’ Day marketing campaign ideas to try: Use support conversations to gather data before Singles’ Day. Let’s say a shopper messages your AI customer agent to ask whether a sold-out serum will restock before 11/11. That exchange can update their profile to include them in a Singles’ Day promo segment, so you can send them a personalized back-in-stock alert. Segment your lists based on interests like self-care, travel, or independent living, then use dynamic content in your messages to highlight products based on a customer’s past browsing or purchase behavior. One person might see a luxe candle set, for example, while another gets a coffee kit. Create irresistible bundles, like a “Self-care Sunday set,” “Solo spa night kit,” or “Treat yourself trio.” Product bundles not only have the potential to boost average order value (AOV), but can also help customers feel like they’re getting something curated just for them. Send a “self-love discount” text message to customers who are marked as single in their profiles or have shown solo-purchasing patterns. Even a cheeky subject line or text message like “It’s called self-love, and you deserve it” can go a long way. Extend the personalization to on-site experiences. When a solo shopper who’s been browsing self-care products lands on your site, their self-serve hub experience can surface Singles’ Day products for potential wishlisting. Singles’ Day marketing example: Dermalogica offers product bundles In this Singles’ Day marketing example, skincare brand Dermalogica skips a sitewide discount in favor of a cleansing set product bundle, priced 28% off with a free gift of a 4-piece self-care set. Rather than pushing every product to every subscriber, they likely focused on shoppers who would want to treat themselves, like big spenders or frequent buyers. Subject line: Limited Supply❣️3 FREE minis + gua sha Image source: Milled 2. Gamify your Singles’ Day campaign Singles’ Day discounts are a huge hit in Asia, but the holiday is also so popular because it often makes shopping feel like a game. If you can bring that same energy to your own campaigns, you’re more likely to create an experience customers can’t help but get involved with. Here are some gamified Singles’ Day marketing campaign ideas to try: Add a spin-to-win form to your site in the week leading up to 11/11. These are great for collecting email addresses and phone numbers, building hype, and making the shopping journey more exciting. Launch a Singles’ Day quiz with AI. Use AI to build the questions, logic, and product recommendations for a conversational quiz with your AI customer agent. When a shopper generates results from the quiz, follow-up messages and on-site experiences speak to corresponding preferences. You can also pair this with a themed discount tied to each person’s quiz results. Turn engagement into a game. Run a giveaway where customers earn entries by completing actions, like signing up, sharing with a friend, or adding something to their wishlist. You can also run a "Comment to unlock" campaign where anyone who comments with a keyword like “single” gets an automatic reply with a call to action (CTA) to sign up for access to exclusive codes. Send interactive mobile messages. Interactive formats like RCS support product carousels and tappable choices. For Singles’ Day, you can send a “Pick your treat” RCS message with 3 tappable gifts, like a mystery discount, a free add-on, or early access to your Singles' Day drop. Singles’ Day marketing example: Campus Shoes runs an Instagram giveaway In this Singles’ Day marketing example, footwear brand Campus Shoes promotes a #DamnGoodShoes giveaway on Instagram. Shoppers can win a pair of sneakers by commenting with a movie title or song that sums up their single life, tagging their single friends, and following Campus Shoes accounts. Th...

blogs.title: 6 Halloween Marketing Campaigns with Real Brand Examples (2026)
blogs.author: Tiff Regaudie
blogs.content: Use Halloween to sharpen BFCM Generated by Klaviyo AI The article explains how to use Halloween email and SMS campaigns to collect customer data, test discount strategies, and refine messaging ahead of Black Friday Cyber Monday. It highlights six examples that show how social proof, segmentation, urgency, and SMS bundles can improve Q4 performance and personalization. Leverage social proof: Feature reviews instead of or alongside discounts in Halloween campaigns to build trust and set up stronger product promotion for BFCM. Collect actionable data: Design Halloween interactions, like playful CTA choices, to gather zero- and first-party data that informs more targeted segments later in Q4. Refine brand and urgency: Use Halloween to test bolder creative, countdown timers, and urgency tactics that reveal which subscribers respond to storytelling versus time-limited offers. Test discount strategies: Experiment with targeted offers and tiers, such as BOGO-style promotions, to identify effective discount levels and audiences before BFCM. Reward SMS subscribers: Offer Halloween-themed early access bundles via SMS to capitalize on high-intent subscribers and accelerate planned purchases. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary If your brand sells makeup , clothing , or food and beverages , your Halloween marketing strategy may be a given. But there’s plenty of spend to go around if you don’t fit neatly into these categories. Even more important, Halloween is a great testing ground for the most lucrative shopping event of the year: Black Friday Cyber Monday (BFCM). And now, the shift towards autonomous marketing means a small team can have a more successful and less stressful October. Here are 6 Halloween marketing campaign ideas with real examples from brands. Align your marketing campaigns with relevant holidays and year-round celebrations. Get your marketing campaign calendar 1. Collect Halloween reviews to build social proof for BFCM According to Klaviyo’s 2025 Future of Consumer Marketing Report , reviews and feedback are more influential to a first purchase than competitive pricing and discounts. So, before you start discounting for your Halloween campaign, consider leaning more heavily on product reviews instead. This strategy, of course, depends on whether you already have good social proof for the product you intend to push during BFCM. Collect reviews year-round with automated request flows , which incentivize customers to review products they recently purchased and can even encourage reviews that contain specific details. That way, you always have a library of holiday-relevant reviews to pull from for your Halloween campaigns. When you’re ready to deploy those reviews as part of any campaign, that’s easiest when they live in the same CRM that houses your customer data. That way, your social proof can line up with any one customer’s browsing or purchase history. If your products aren’t an obvious Halloween buy, use the holiday to offer a discount in exchange for a review on a product you plan to feature during BFCM. Your BFCM self will thank you later. Halloween marketing example: Happy Wax uses reviews to highlight product benefits Happy Wax , a brand that sells wax warmers and candles, uses their Halloween marketing to feature social proof from a few satisfied customers. The first review in the series is specifically Halloween-themed, which means the brand made the effort to collect social proof that fits a purpose. To collect this kind of social proof, you can add custom questions to your review requests. A question like, "How did this product help you celebrate Halloween?" when a customer bought from a Halloween discount can help your customers get specific with their review. Subject line: Get Spooky with BLOOD MOON 🌝 Image source: Milled 2. Answer Halloween shopper questions with an AI customer agent Halloween traffic brings a wave of questions: what will ship on time for the party, what size to order, and what costume elements pair with what. Left unanswered, those questions can turn into abandoned carts. But when you answer some of these simple questions at scale, you can turn them into holiday revenue more quickly. For example, a customer might text about a recent order days before Halloween to ask whether the product will ship in time for their party. An AI customer agent can pull from your brand’s shipping policy and customer data to personalize an answer, no matter what time they reach out. Halloween marketing example: Naked Wardrobe answers customer questions with an AI agent Shapewear and streetwear brand Naked Wardrobe wanted to create a concierge experience for their website. The brand was using AI for customer service on their site, but it could only recognize and quickly resolve a few pre-set queries. It also had limited contextual information on customers. Now, Naked Wardrobe is using an AI customer agent that can answer questions like a skilled salesperson. Trained on their website and documentation, it can handle post-purchase service queries about order status and returns, as well as pre-purchase product recommendation requests. In this Halloween marketing example, Naked Wardrobe’s AI agent recommends an outfit for a potential customer looking for warm and witchy Halloween costume options. Image source: Naked Wardrobe When people click on one over the other, they might see a creepy image. Or a funny one. Or a cute one. It’s a Halloween Choose Your Own Adventure that ends in delight—and, most importantly, a vibe check on the brand’s audience. 3. Draft Halloween campaigns faster with an AI marketing agent If you don't want to compete on price with heavy discounting, increasing your top-of-mind brand awareness may be your best bet ahead of BFCM. That could mean testing bolder versions of your brand voice. Halloween is a great holiday for this, since it’s cheeky to begin with. With an AI marketing agent , you can describe the tone you want in a prompt, and it drafts the content, builds the customer segments, and determines send times across channels. Here are some example prompts to start with: Test a bolder voice. “Write a Halloween email for subscribers who have browsed our skincare category but not purchased in the last 60 days. Position our bestselling serum as a potion. Be dry and a little witchy, no forced puns. Lead with the product benefit and one clear CTA, then draft a text message follow-up for anyone who opens but doesn't click.” Build from a product image. “Here's a photo of our top-selling product, a candle that smells like a wood cabin. Create a Halloween email based on this photo for customers who haven’t bought from us since last October. The header copy should emphasize the magical nature of this candle as customers prep for the most enchanted day of the year.” Try some humor. “Write a Halloween 'lick or treat' campaign for our dog treats. Keep it kooky and short. Give repeat purchasers early access to the Halloween bundle as a thank-you, and give lapsed customers a limited-time discount with more urgency to come back before it sells out. I need an email and text message with follow ups for each segment.” According to Klaviyo's 2026 Match Day Ready Report , 66% of B2C teams missed at least one cultural moment in the past year because they couldn't move fast enough. During Halloween, testing new ways to decrease campaign execution time can help get you ready for BFCM. Halloween marketing example: Surreal leans into the chaos Cereal brand Surreal built this Halloween marketing email around a deadpan 10-step survival guide for a demon apocalypse. The humor is dry, the logic is absurd, and the product mention is buried naturally into the bit ("demons hate cereal"). Subject line: All hell breaks loose 🎃🦇 Image source: Really Good Emails 4.
